problem_data.story:
The holiday party at the Valleyview branch of QuantumMed Solutions was threatening to become more legendary than usual this December.

The virtual reality division manager had already collapsed after attempting to demonstrate the new immersive healthcare training module while intoxicated. When he stumbled into the server rack, Teresa Gray, who managed the biotechnology research department, had screamed: "He'll crash the entire system!"

One out of every three presentations about breakthrough genetic engineering techniques had remained unfinished, because each had reminded someone else of another research project they wanted to discuss.

The recently approved synthetic compounds which affected neural receptors three times faster had driven away twinges of conscience about unfinished year-end reports and mandatory ethics training modules.

The star salesperson for medical AI systems and the gentleman who was in charge of facility maintenance were putting on a display of competitive data visualization in one corner of the main laboratory. The maintenance supervisor had fifty pounds less experience than the AI salesperson's customary opponent. So the climax of one particularly aggressive chart animation did not simply overturn the supervisor's monitor. It glided through the air, crashing with a very loud thump against the wall.

No one was hurt. But the impact knocked the hallowed portrait of Dr. Helena QuantumMed, co-founder, from its mounting. It shattered impressively as its protective glass splintered against the floor.

The noise caused a temporary lull in the festivities. Several employees even felt a passing suspicion that things might be getting out of hand.

"It's all in the spirit of scientific collaboration!" cried Daniel Wallace, the assistant director of operations. Since he was the highest executive present, worries vanished. Everyone felt fine. There was a scurry to shove the broken glass out of sight and to turn more attention to another type of beakers.

Daniel himself, acting by reflex, attempted to return the portrait to its place until new glass could be obtained. But the fall had damaged the frame at one corner and it wouldn't hang straight.

"We'd better store Dr. QuantumMed away for safekeeping until after the holiday," he told a small, blonde research assistant who was beneath his attention on any working day.

With the proper mixture of respect and holiday cheer, he lifted the heavy picture out of its frame. A yellowed envelope slipped to the floor as the picture came free. Daniel rolled the picture like a scroll and put it into a storage cabinet, for later attention. Then he looked around for a drink that would make him feel even better.

A data entry clerk in the clinical trials department wasn't used to liquor. She picked up the envelope and looked around vaguely for the document scanner.

"Hell, Mira, you aren't working!" someone shouted at her. "Have another!"

Mira Parsons snapped out of it. She giggled, suppressed a ladylike hiccup and returned to reality. Looking at the envelope, she said: "Oh, I see. They must have stuck it in to stabilize the frame. Gee, it's old."

Daniel had refreshed himself. He decided that he liked Mira's voice. To hear more of it, he said to her: "I'll bet that's been in there ever since the picture was mounted. There's a company legend that this portrait was installed the day this branch opened, ninety years ago."

"I didn't know the company ever used manila envelopes like this." Mira turned it over in her hands. The ancient adhesive crackled as she did so. The flap popped open and an old-fashioned order form fell out.

Daniel's eyes widened. He bent, reached painfully over his expanding midsection and picked up the order form.

"This thing has never been processed!" Raising his voice, he shouted jovially, "Hey, people! You're all terminated! Here's an order that QuantumMed never filled! We can't have such negligence. This poor customer has waited ninety years for their medical equipment!"

Mira was reading aloud the scrawled words on the order form:

"Advanced diagnostic scanner. Pediatric health monitor. Gene therapy starter kit. Adaptive medication dispenser for elderly patient." She turned to the assistant director, struck with an idea for the first time in her young life. "Let's fill this order right now!"

"The poor customer must be deceased by now," he objected, secretly angry that he hadn't thought of such a fine party stunt himself. Then he brightened. "Unless—" he said it loud enough for the employees to anticipate a grand proposal and the room grew quiet—"unless we broke the rules just once and used the temporal displacement field on a humanitarian mission!"

There was a silence. Finally, from an anonymous voice in one corner: "Would the field work over ninety years? We were always told that it must be used only for product recalls within three days."

"Then let's find out!" Daniel downed the rest of his drink and pulled a batch of access cards from his pocket. "Someone head down to the warehouse. Tell the security officer that it's on my authority. Hunt up the equipment that's on the order. Get the best of everything. Ignore the catalogue numbers—they've changed a hundred times in all these years."

Mira was still deciphering the form. Now she let out a little squeal of excitement.

"Look, Daniel! The name on this order—it's my great-great-grandmother! Isn't that wonderful? I was just a little girl when my grandmother told me stories about her. I remember that my grandmother never bought anything from QuantumMed because of some incident her grandmother had once with the firm. My mother didn't want me to come to work here because of that."

Daniel put his arm around Mira in a way that he intended to look mentorly. It didn't. "Well, now. Since it's your relative, let's delight the old woman. We'll give her the finest equipment we have in stock!"

A warehouse technician appeared at Daniel's elbow, tablet in hand. "Sir, I've located most items on the list. The scanner, the health monitor, the medication dispenser—all available in our premium line."

"Excellent! Pack them up."

The technician hesitated. "There's one complication. The third item on the list—we don't carry anything by that exact name anymore. Our inventory system shows we have NeuroSync neural enhancement units in that product category now. Should I substitute?"

"Perfect! Send whatever's closest. The old woman won't know the difference after ninety years." Daniel waved his hand dismissively and reached for another drink.

---

Ruth Wheeler was returning from filing a complaint at the local QuantumMed office when she found the large parcel on her doorstep in Glendale, Wendria. She put her hands on her hips and stared suspiciously at the container.

"The minute I submit a formal complaint about you, you materialize!" she told the parcel. She nudged her toe irritably against the silver wrappings that were sealed with a half-transparent binding material she had never seen before.

The label was addressed in a wandering scrawl, a sharp contrast to the impersonal printing on the customary QuantumMed packages. But the familiar FRAGILE MEDICAL EQUIPMENT sticker was pasted onto the box, indicating to the delivery person that the contents required careful handling.

Ruth sighed and picked up her bundle. With a last look at the lovely spring afternoon and the quiet suburban landscape of Glendale, she went into the house.

Five-year-old Isabel heard the box humming. She toddled up on energetic legs and grabbed her grandmother's skirt. "Want!" she said decisively.

"Your medication dispenser ought to be here," Ruth said. She found scissors in her sewing box, tossed a cushion onto the floor, sat on it, and began to open the parcel.

"Now I'll have to submit another form to explain that they should disregard my complaint," she told her granddaughter. "And by the time they receive my second form, they'll have responded to my first form. Then they'll write again." Out of consideration for Isabel, she omitted the expletives that she wanted to add.

The translucent binding was too tough for the scissors. Ruth was about to hunt for a laser cutter when Isabel clutched at an intersection of the cord and yanked. The binding sprang away from the carton as if it were programmed. The wrappings flapped open.

"There!" Isabel said.

Ruth repressed an irrational urge to scold her granddaughter. Instead, she tossed the wrappings aside and removed the lid from the carton. A slightly crushed thin cardboard box lay on top. Ruth pulled out the medication dispenser and examined it carefully. Then she groaned.

It was silver and she had ordered white. It didn't remotely resemble the dispenser she had admired from the QuantumMed catalogue illustration. Moreover, the device had unusual protrusions that no standard medication dispenser should have.

But Isabel was delighted. "Mine!" she shrilled, grabbing for the device.

"It's probably the wrong model, too," Ruth said, examining the control panel. "Let's identify as many defects to complain about as we can."

The device seemed to activate when Isabel touched it. A soft blue glow emanated from its surface. Isabel was radiant for a moment. Then her small face sobered and she started to look vacantly at the distant wall.

"We'll have to return it," Ruth said, "and get the one we ordered."

She tried to take it from Isabel's hands, but the child resisted violently. Ruth grabbed her granddaughter's wrists, held them firmly and tried to pry the device away. It seemed to be adhered somehow. When Ruth released the child's wrists to examine the device more closely, Isabel stepped backward, then began to levitate three feet above the ground. She landed just before she collided with the far wall.

Isabel looked scared until she saw her grandmother's face. Then she squealed in delight.

Ruth's legs were rubber. She was shaking her head and wobbling uncertainly toward her granddaughter when the door opened behind her.

"It's me," her son Felix said. "Slow day at the research institute, so I came home early."

"Felix! I'm experiencing some kind of hallucination or something. Isabel just—"

"Mom! Your complaint was resolved? Good. What's this thing?" He was looking at a small cylindrical device he had pulled from the carton. Its surface contained a single word: NEUROSYNC. The device hummed when he held it.

"Is this the diagnostic scanner? I've never seen technology like this. And there's no power source visible."

"I don't know," Ruth said. "Felix, listen. A moment ago, Isabel—"

He peered into the box for an instruction manual, uselessly. "They must have made an error. It looks like some kind of experimental biotechnology equipment."

He placed the NeuroSync onto the coffee table and delved into the carton again. Isabel was still in his arms.

"That's the scanner, I think," he said, looking at the next object. It had a lovely, streamlined shape, multiple sensor arrays and a connection port for a power outlet.

"That's curious," Ruth mused, her mind distracted from Isabel for a moment. "It looks terribly advanced. Maybe they sent a premium model instead of the standard scanner."

The bottom of the carton contained the health monitor that they had ordered for Isabel. Ruth glanced at its sleek interface and counted silently: one scanner, one health monitor, one medication dispenser, one mysterious cylinder. She frowned, mentally checking items against her original order. Three of the four items seemed accounted for, though wildly different from what she'd expected. But that cylindrical thing with NEUROSYNC printed on it—she had no idea what category of medical equipment it was supposed to represent.

"Felix, about Isabel. Put her down a minute and observe what she does."

Felix stared at his mother and placed the child onto the carpet. Isabel began to walk, then rose and again levitated, this time toward the coffee table on which the NeuroSync rested.

His jaw dropped. "My God! Mom, what—"

Ruth was staring, too, but not at her granddaughter. "Felix! The coffee table! It used to be brown!"

The coffee table was a vivid shade of blue. A neon, demanding, screaming blue that clashed horribly with the soft earth tones in which Ruth had furnished the room.

"That cylindrical thing must be emitting something," Felix said, his background in complexity science kicking in. "But did you see Isabel when she—"

Ruth's frazzled nerves carried a frantic order to her muscles. She jumped up, strode to the coffee table and picked up the NeuroSync with two fingers. She tossed it to Felix. Immediately, she regretted her action.

"Drop it!" she yelled. "Maybe it'll alter your neural patterns, too!"

Felix kicked the coffee table into the hall closet, tossed the NeuroSync in after it and shut the door firmly. As the door closed, he saw the entire interior of the dark closet illuminate into a wet-sapphire blue.

When he turned back to Ruth, she was staring at her left wrist. The medical monitoring bracelet that the hospital had given her years ago was a brilliant blue, shedding its soft glow over her forearm up to the elbow.

Ruth felt the panic building up inside her. She opened her mouth to scream, then put her hand in front of her mouth to suppress it, finally jerked the hand away to prevent the glowing bracelet from turning her teeth blue.

She collapsed into Felix's arms, babbling incomprehensibly about epistemology and the nature of reality.

He said: "It's all right. There must be some kind of anti-gravity field or something in that medication dispenser. I'll attach a weight to Isabel's belt and that'll hold her down until we can remove the device. Don't worry. And that blue emission or whatever it is will dissipate."

Ruth immediately felt better. She put her hands behind her back, pulled off her bracelet and slipped it into her pocket. Felix was sentimental about her removing it.

"I'll prepare dinner," she said, trying to keep her voice steady. "Maybe you'd better start a complaint form to QuantumMed. Let's go into the kitchen, Isabel."

Ruth strode resolutely toward the rear of the house. She kept her eyes determinedly off the tinge of blue that was showing through her pocket and didn't dare look back at her granddaughter's unsettling means of propulsion.

A half-hour later, when the meal was almost ready, two things happened: Pablo Fuller came home from the university through the back door and a strange voice said from the front of the house, "Unauthorized access detected."

Ruth stared at her grandson. He stared back at her, the pediatric health monitor under his arm.

She went into the front room. Her son was standing with fists on hips, looking at the front door, chuckling. "Most sophisticated security system I've seen in a long time. That voice you heard was the new diagnostic scanner. I installed it while you were in the kitchen. Did you hear what happened when old Mr. Brennan out there approached the entrance?"

"Oh. Something like those smart home systems with voice warnings, like 'Motion detected.' Well, if there's some kind of AI in there repeating that message, you'd better deactivate that function. It might get annoying after a while. And it might offend someone."

Ruth went to the door and turned the handle. The door didn't open. The figure of Mr. Brennan, half-visible through the heavy curtain, shifted impatiently on the porch.

Felix yanked at the doorknob. It didn't yield for him, either. He looked up at the scanner, which he had installed just above the upper part of the door frame.

"Strange," he said, applying his knowledge of information theory. "That isn't in contact with the door mechanism itself. I don't see how it can prevent the door from opening."

Ruth put her mouth close to the glass, shouting: "Won't you come to the back door, Mr. Brennan? This one is malfunctioning."

"I just wanted to borrow some medical supplies," the man called from the porch. "I realize that I'm a terrible bother." But he walked down the front steps and disappeared around the side of the house.

"Biometric authentication required." The well-modulated voice from the small scanner box threatened to penetrate every corner of the house. Ruth looked doubtfully at her son's lips. They weren't moving.

"If this is some kind of prank—" she began icily.

"I'll have to order another scanner just like this one, for the lab," Felix said. "But you'd better let the old fellow in. No use letting him get upset."

The back door was already open, because it was a warm day. The screen door had no latch, held closed by a simple spring. Ruth pushed it open when Mr. Brennan trudged up the three back steps, and smiled at her neighbor.

"I'm so sorry you had to walk around the house. It's been a rather chaotic day in an awful lot of ways."

Something seemed to impede Mr. Brennan as he came to the threshold. He frowned and pushed his frail frame against something invisible. It apparently yielded abruptly, because he staggered forward into the kitchen, nearly falling. He stared grimly at Ruth and looked suspiciously behind him.

"The children have some new equipment," Ruth improvised hastily. "Isabel is so excited over a new device that she's positively euphoric. Let's see now—it was medical supplies that you need, wasn't it?"

"I already have them," Pablo said, handing a small package to his grandmother. The boy turned back to the health monitor which he had spread over the kitchen table, studying its interface with fascination.

"Excitement isn't good for me," Mr. Brennan said testily, his understanding of social dynamics clearly limited. "I've had a lot of health problems in my life. I like peace and stability."

"Your wife is better?"

"Worse. I'm sure I don't know why everything happens to me." Mr. Brennan edged toward the hall, trying to peer into the front of the house. Ruth stood squarely in front of the door leading to the hall. Defeated, Mr. Brennan left. A muffled series of beeps, mixed with a few faint diagnostic readings, came from the scanner-box when he crossed the threshold.

Ruth went into the hall to order Felix to disconnect the scanner. She nearly collided with him, coming in the other direction.

"Where did this come from?" Felix held a small object in the palm of his hand, keeping it away from his body. A few drops of something viscous were dripping from his fingers. The object looked remarkably like a miniature brain. It was human-size, complete with cortical folds, neural pathways and rather prominent blood vessels.

"Hey, that's mine," Pablo said. "You know, this is an unusual health monitor. That was in it. But there aren't instructions on how it operates."

"Well, put it away," Ruth told Pablo sharply. "It's disturbing."

Felix laid the brain-device on the table and walked away. The device rolled from the smooth, level table, bounced twice when it hit the floor, then rolled along, six inches behind him. He turned and kicked at it. The device rolled nimbly out of the path of the kick.

"Felix, I think we've made poor Mr. Brennan uncomfortable," Ruth said. "He's so upset over his wife's health and he thinks we're being inhospitable."

Felix didn't hear her. He strode to the health monitor, followed at a safe distance by the brain-device, and picked up the box.

"Hey, watch out!" Pablo cried. A small scanning wand fell from the box, landed on its side and its sensor flashed on, throwing a beam of light across Felix's hands.

Pablo retrieved the wand and turned it off while Felix glanced through an instruction manual, frowning.

"This equipment is too advanced for a twelve-year-old boy," Felix told his mother, his expertise in theoretical modeling evident. "I don't know why you ordered such a thing." He tossed the manual into the empty box.

"I'm going to return it, if you don't damage it," she replied. "Look at the marks you made on the instructions." The black marks stood out clearly against the glossy, coated paper.

Felix looked at his hands. "I didn't do it," he said, pressing his clean fingertips against the kitchen table.

Black marks, a full set of them, stood out against the sparkling polished table's surface.

"I think the BioScanner did it," Pablo said, using the term from the manual. "The instructions say you've got to be very careful with it, because its effects persist for an extended duration."

Felix began scrubbing his hands vigorously at the sink. Ruth watched him silently, until she saw his marks appear on the faucet, the soap dispenser and the towel. She began to reprimand him for making such a mess, when Isabel levitated into the kitchen. The girl was wearing a different outfit.

"My God!" Ruth forgot her language before the children. "She changed clothes herself. Where did she get that outfit?"

Ruth examined the garment. She didn't recognize it as sleepwear. But in cut and design, it was suspiciously like the medication dispenser interface that had arrived in the parcel. Her heart sank.

She picked up the child, felt the elevated temperature, and said: "Felix, I think it's the same device. It must adapt its appearance or something based on the user's physiological state. It seems impossible, but—" She shrugged mutely. "And I think Isabel's running a fever. I'm going to put her to bed."

She looked worriedly into the reddened eyes of the small girl, who whimpered on the way to the bedroom. Ruth carried her up the stairs, keeping her balance with difficulty, as Isabel threatened to float upward out of her arms.

The whole family decided that rest might be a good idea, soon after dinner. When the lights went out, the house seemed to be nearly normal. Felix put on a pair of gloves and threw a blanket over the brain-device. Pablo rigged up barriers to warn visitors from the front porch. Ruth put small earplugs into her ears, because she didn't like the rhythmic hum, soft but persistent, that emerged from the hall closet where the NeuroSync sat. Isabel was whimpering occasionally in her sleep.

When daylight entered her room, Isabel's outfit had transformed back into the medication dispenser interface. But the little girl was too sick to get out of bed. She wasn't hungry, her breathing was labored, and she had a persistent cough. Felix called the doctor before going to work.

The only positive thing about the morning for Ruth was the fact that the NeuroSync had quieted down some time in the night. After she got Pablo to school, she gingerly opened the closet door. The NeuroSync was now glowing a bright pink and seemed slightly larger. Deep violet text stood out on its surface:

"Today is Wednesday. For system maintenance, the NeuroSync will not operate today."

Ruth stared at the strange device. She had spent hours the previous night trying to recall every item on her original order form, cross-referencing what had actually arrived. The scanner was present, though far more advanced than expected. The health monitor had come, bizarre as it was. The medication dispenser was attached to Isabel. But this cylinder—she had never ordered anything called NeuroSync. She had ordered something else entirely in that fourth slot on the form, something her doctor had specifically recommended for her arthritis. Whatever this glowing cylinder was supposed to be, it certainly wasn't that.

The mail carrier brought a letter from QuantumMed. Ruth stared stupidly at the envelope, until she realized that this wasn't an impossibly quick response to the complaint she had filed yesterday. It must have crossed in transit her complaint about the non-delivery of the order. She tore open the envelope and read:

"We regret to inform you that your order cannot be processed until the outstanding balance you owe us has been reduced. From the attached statement, you will readily ascertain that the payment of $1,247.89 will enable you to resume the purchasing of medical equipment on credit. We shall process your recent order as soon...."

Ruth crumpled the letter and threw it into the recycling bin, knowing perfectly well that it would need to be retrieved for Felix after work tonight. She had just decided to contact QuantumMed's complaint department when the phone rang.

"I'm afraid I must ask you to come down to the school, Mrs. Wheeler," a voice said. "Your grandson is in trouble. He claims that it's connected with something that his family gave him."

"My grandson?" Ruth asked incredulously. "Pablo?"

"Yes. It's a small device that looks like a medical scanner. Your grandson insists that he didn't know it would make clothing transparent. He claims it was just an accident that he tried it out when he was walking by the gymnasium during physical education. We've had to request emergency blankets from every family in the neighborhood. Pablo has always been a good student and we believe that we can handle this discreetly without media publicity involving his name, if you'll—"

"I'll be right down," Ruth said. "I mean I won't be right down. I've got a sick child here. Don't do anything until I contact my son. And I'm sorry for Pablo. I mean I'm sorry for the students, and for the teachers, too. I'm sorry for—for everything. Goodbye."

Just as she hung up the telephone, the scanner rang with an alert. It chimed with a normal tone, then began to play soft diagnostic readings. Ruth opened the door without difficulty, to admit Dr. Zara Francis.

"You aren't going to believe me, Doctor," Ruth said while she took the child's temperature, "but we can't remove that device from Isabel."

"Children can be stubborn sometimes." Dr. Francis whistled softly when she looked at the thermometer. "She's quite ill. I need a blood sample before I attempt to move her. Let me examine her."

Isabel had been mumbling semi-deliriously. She made no effort to resist as the doctor picked her up. But when she raised a component of the device and began to detach it, Isabel screamed.

The doctor released the device and looked in perplexity at the point where it interfaced with Isabel's body.

"It's apparently an adverse reaction to some new kind of biotechnology. But I don't understand why the device won't detach. It's not physically bonded."

"Don't bother trying," Ruth said miserably, her understanding of healthcare policy telling her this would be complicated. "Just cut it off."

Dr. Francis pulled medical scissors from her bag and attempted to separate a component. When she had cut partway through, she gently began to peel back the edges of the material. Isabel writhed and kicked, then collapsed in unconsciousness. The physician smoothly restored the components back into place.

She looked helpless as she said to Ruth: "I don't know quite what to do. The tissue starts to hemorrhage when I manipulate the interface. She'd experience severe trauma if I removed it forcibly. But it's such an extreme reaction that it may harm her, if we leave it in contact with her body."

The NeuroSync's hum suddenly began rhythmically from the lower part of the house. Ruth clutched the side of the chair, trying to keep herself under control. A siren wailed somewhere down the street, grew louder rapidly, suddenly going silent at the peak of its crescendo.

Dr. Francis glanced outside the window. "An emergency vehicle. Looks as if they're stopping here."

"Oh, no," Ruth breathed. "Something's happened to Felix."

"It certainly will," Felix said grimly, walking into the bedroom. "I won't have employment if I can't remove this substance from my fingers. Black marks on everything I touch. I can't handle laboratory equipment or interact with research subjects. How's the child? What's the emergency vehicle doing out front?"

"They're going to the next house down the street," the physician said. "Has there been illness there?"

Felix held up his hands, palms toward the doctor. "What's wrong with me? My fingers appear normal. But they leave black marks on everything I touch."

The doctor looked closely at the fingertips, applying statistical inference. "Every human has natural secretions on the skin. That's how forensic scientists get results with their identification techniques. But I've never encountered chromatization, in this context. Better not attempt to handle sensitive materials until you've consulted a dermatological specialist."

Ruth was peering through the window, curious about the emergency vehicle despite her own troubles. She saw two paramedics carry Mrs. Brennan, motionless and pale, on a stretcher from the house next door into the vehicle. A third member of the crew was struggling with a disheveled Mr. Brennan at the door. Shouts that sounded like "Negligence!" came sharply through the window.

"I know those paramedics," Dr. Francis said. She opened the window. "Hey, Marcus! What's wrong?"

The front paramedic looked up. "I don't know. This woman's critically ill. I think her husband is experiencing psychological distress."

Mr. Brennan had broken free. He rushed halfway down the sidewalk, gesticulating wildly to nobody in particular.

"It's negligence!" he screamed. "Medical negligence again! She's been harmed by faulty equipment! She's going to die! It means legal consequences!"

The paramedic grabbed him again. This time he administered a mild sedative to calm him.

"Come back to this house as soon as you deliver her," Dr. Francis shouted to the crew. "We've got a very sick child up here."

"I was concerned this would happen," Felix said, his knowledge of behavioral economics evident in his analysis. "The poor man already has lost two wives to medical complications. If this one is ill, it's no wonder he thinks that somebody is responsible for medical negligence."

Pablo stuck his head around the bedroom door. His grandmother stared unbelievingly for a moment, then advanced on him threateningly. Something in his face restrained her, just as she was about to start reprimanding him.

"I got something important to tell you," Pablo said rapidly, ready to retreat. "I escaped from the principal's office and came home. I need to tell you what I did."

"I heard all about what you did," Ruth said, advancing again. "And you're not going to evade responsibility."

"Give me a chance to explain something. Downstairs. So she won't hear," Pablo ended in a whisper, nodding toward the doctor.

Ruth looked doubtfully at Felix, then followed Pablo down the stairs. The scanner was monotonously saying in a monotone: "Access denied, access denied, unauthorized entry prohibited."

"Why did you do it?" Ruth asked Pablo, her anger suddenly slumping into weary sadness. "People will suspect you of being disturbed for the rest of your life. You can't possibly explain—"

"Don't worry about the students' clothing," Pablo said, "because it was only an accident. The really important thing is something else I did before I left the house."

Felix, cursing softly, hurried past them on the way to answer the knocking. He ignored the scanner's warnings.

"I forgot about it," Pablo continued, "when that scanning device accidentally activated. Then when they confined me in the principal's office, I had time to think, and I remembered. I put some white substance from the health monitor into those medical supplies we lent Mr. Brennan last night. I just wanted to observe what would happen. I don't know exactly what effect—"

"He put substance in the medical supplies?" A deep, authoritative voice came from the front of the house. Mother and grandson looked through the hall. A police officer stood on the threshold of the front door. "I heard that! The man next door claims that his wife has been poisoned by medical negligence. Young man, I'm going to have to take you into custody."

The officer stepped over the threshold. A blue flash darted from the scanner box, striking him squarely on the chest. The officer staggered back, sitting down abruptly on the porch. A scent of ozone drifted through the house.

"Close the door, close the door," the scanner was announcing urgently.

"Where's that emergency vehicle?" Dr. Francis yelled from the top of the steps. "The child's condition is deteriorating."

Ruth sank into a chair, overwhelmed. She thought about the copy of her original order form, still filed in her desk drawer upstairs—four items carefully selected with her doctor's help. Three of them had arrived in some form, however strange. The fourth, the treatment she had hoped would finally ease the stiffness in her hands that made even holding Isabel difficult some mornings, had been replaced by that unsettling cylinder in the closet. QuantumMed had failed her again, just as they had failed her grandmother all those years ago.
